title: The Problem of Evil
objective: After this level you can explain the problem of evil as philosophers state it and the free will reply offered by Augustine and, later, Alvin Plantinga.
summary: The problem of evil, attributed to Epicurus and sharpened by Mackie, asks how God and evil can coexist; Augustine and Plantinga reply with free will, and critics answer with natural evil.

cards.headline: If God could stop suffering and wanted to, why is there any?
cards.body: Philosophers call this the problem of evil. Critics of belief in God have sharpened it since Epicurus’s name was attached to it, and theists have answered it just as long.

cards.headline: Epicurus’s old questions
cards.body: The dilemma is traditionally attributed to Epicurus, though that attribution is uncertain. Hume’s character Philo puts it in three questions: “Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? then is he impotent. Is he able, but not willing? then is he malevolent. Is he both able and willing? whence then is evil?”

cards.headline: A contradiction?
cards.body: In 1955 J. L. Mackie turned this into a charge of inconsistency. Theists say God is all-powerful, all-knowing and perfectly good, and they agree evil exists. Mackie argued those four claims can’t all be true together, so religious belief is not just unsupported but “positively irrational.” On his reasoning, an all-powerful God could prevent evil, and a perfectly good one would want to.

cards.headline: The free will reply
cards.body: Augustine held that free will is a great good, though not an absolute one, and that its misuse is the source of moral evil. Alvin Plantinga (1974) built this into a defense: a world where free creatures do more good than evil is more valuable, and God can’t cause creatures to do only right freely. It doesn’t claim to know God’s actual reasons, only to show there’s no contradiction.

mascot.line: Keep this: Plantinga’s defense aims only to show God and evil aren’t contradictory, not to explain why each evil happens.

cards.headline: Critics reply
cards.body: Critics answer that much suffering is nobody’s choice: disease, famine, earthquakes. Free will might explain cruelty, but why would freedom need earthquakes? Mackie also asked why an all-powerful God couldn’t make people who act freely but always choose the good. Plantinga agrees such a world is possible, but says whether it happens depends on what free creatures would do, not on God alone.

cards.headline: The Problem of Evil: the big picture
learned: Epicurus’s old questions about God and evil
Critics: natural evil isn’t anyone’s choice

questions.prompt: According to Augustine, where does moral evil come from?

options.label: A flaw in how God made the world
options.rationale: He traced it to free choice.

questions.explanation: Augustine held that free will is a great good that can be misused, and that misuse is the source of moral evil.

questions.prompt: Why does Plantinga say God could not simply make creatures who freely do only good?

options.label: Because God cannot know what any creature will choose
Because some evil is needed to keep the world in balance
Because Mackie had shown such creatures are impossible
Because causing them to do only good means they don’t do it freely

questions.explanation: If God causes creatures to do only right, they don’t do it freely; so a world with free, good creatures isn’t up to God alone.

questions.prompt: Mackie lays out claims about God’s power, knowledge and goodness to support his conclusion. What does Level 1 call such supporting reasons?

options.label: Experiments
options.rationale: Level 1 says these questions can’t be settled by experiment alone.

options.label: Aggregates
options.rationale: That’s Level 8’s word for parts of a person.

options.label: Forms
options.rationale: That’s Plato’s word for perfect realities.

questions.explanation: Philosophy’s main tool is the argument: reasons, called premises, laid out to support a conclusion.
